summary: This RFC explains why some local-area networks used "trailer encapsulations" and describes how they were implemented on various media. It is informational only and the RFC states it is not an official ARPA Internet protocol.

eli5.summary: Some machines put the label at the end of the package instead of the front. This note explains why and how, but says it is not the official way.

questions: why use trailer encapsulation on ethernet
subtitle: Putting variable-length protocol headers after the data so a receiver can keep the data page-aligned and avoid copying it.

tldr.problem: Receiving hosts spend effort copying packet data between memory areas, and varying header sizes stop the data from landing on a page boundary where memory mapping could replace the copy.
tldr.mechanism: A sender moves the variable-length headers behind the data, so the data starts at a fixed place and has a size that is a multiple of 512 bytes, and the link-level type field tells the receiver how much data there is.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes the format used by 4.2BSD UNIX and others, but states it is for information only and is NOT an official protocol for the ARPA Internet community.

today: RFC 893 is an informational memo whose status is not given in the record beyond that, and the text itself says it is NOT an official ARPA Internet protocol. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a Trailer Encapsulation Is
sections.content:
A trailer encapsulation is a link-level packet format used by 4.2BSD UNIX, among others. A system may generate one under certain conditions to reduce the number and size of memory-to-memory copy operations that the receiving host performs on a data packet.

Trailers are strictly a link-level format and, when properly implemented, are not visible to higher-level protocol processing. The note describes the formats used on 3 Mb/s Experimental Ethernet, 10 Mb/s Ethernet and 10 Mb/s V2LNI ring networks. The idea was suggested by Greg Chesson and the encapsulation was designed by Bill Joy. The RFC is for information only.
sections.eli5: It is a different way to pack a parcel at the network level: the address stuff goes on the back, so the receiver can grab the contents faster.

sections.title: Why Trailers: Avoiding Copies
sections.content:
An optimal network implementation would do zero copies between a packet arriving in host memory and the data reaching the receiving process. With virtual memory support this can often be done by manipulating the memory hardware instead of copying. In a page-mapped system, the data must be aligned on a page boundary and have a size that is a multiple of the hardware page size.

That is hard when protocol headers vary in size, for example because of different protocols or optional header information. So the trailer scheme takes all possibly variable-length header information and moves it after the data segment, leaving a fixed-size link-level header in front. The sender thereby does its best to let the receiver get page-aligned data.
sections.eli5: If the labels on the front are different sizes, the contents start at a different spot each time. Moving the labels to the back keeps the contents in the same place.

sections.title: Assumptions and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC lists four assumptions behind the argument. The receiver must be willing to accept trailers; the cost of receiving page-aligned data should be comparable to non-aligned data; the variable-length header should be much smaller than the data; and the copying saved must be large enough to justify the extra software complexity.

The first is the weak point. Because trailers are a link-level format, hosts sharing a medium must all accept trailers or never send them. Negotiation per host, perhaps by augmenting the Address Resolution Protocol (RFC 826), was considered but not adopted. The authors say 4.2BSD can switch trailers off at boot time without modifying the operating system source.

For TCP/IP (RFC 791 for IP), the smallest trailer packet generated by a VAX has 512 bytes of data and 40 or more bytes of headers. The authors say supporting trailers took about a dozen lines of code in each network interface driver. They also admit a valid criticism: the receiver must buffer the whole packet before it can recognise the network-level type.
sections.eli5: It only works if both sides agree to do it this way. The authors thought the small extra work was worth it.

sections.title: The Trailer Packet Layout
sections.content:
A trailer packet has three parts: the fixed-size local network header (LH), the data, and the trailer (TH). The formats on the three networks differ only in the header format and the type field values.

On 10 Mb/s Ethernet the type field in LH shows both that the packet is a trailer packet and how long the data is. The types run from 1001 to 1010 hexadecimal (4096 to 4112 decimal): the type is 1000 hex plus the number of 512-byte pages of data. A single trailer packet carries at most 16 pages, or 8192 bytes. The data is normally only user data, with no TCP or IP headers, and its size is always a multiple of 512 bytes.

The receiver locates the trailer using the size in the type field, discards the link-level header and trailer prefix, and remaps the trailing data to the front to rebuild the original network-level packet.
sections.eli5: The front label says how many 512-byte chunks of data are inside, so the receiver knows where the back label begins.

sections.title: The Trailer Itself
sections.content:
The trailer holds the original protocol headers behind a fixed-size prefix that records the type and size of the trailing data. It has three fields:

  • Type (16 bits): the original link-level type that would have been in the header had no trailer been used.
  • Header length (16 bits): the length in bytes of the header data that follows.
  • Original headers (variable): the header information that logically belongs before the data, normally network and transport level headers.
sections.eli5: The back label says what kind of package it really is, how long the address part is, and then holds the address part itself.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Original link-level type of the packet.

fields.name: Header length
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the header data that follows.
